40397:
In 539 BC Cyrus the Great of Persia took Babylon without a major battle. Unlike the Assyrians and Babylonians, the Persians allowed conquered peoples to return home and restore their temples, keeping them loyal and paying taxes. The Cyrus Cylinder, discovered in 1879, records this policy in Babylonian terms (though it does not mention the Jews). Ezra opens with Cyrus' decree, presented as the LORD 'stirring up the spirit of Cyrus' to fulfil Jeremiah's prophecy of seventy years (Ezra 1:1; Jer 29:10).

The first return was led by Sheshbazzar and then Zerubbabel, a grandson of King Jehoiachin, and Jeshua the high priest. About 42,000 people returned (Ezra 2:64), a fraction of the exiles; many stayed in Babylon, which became a major centre of Jewish life for over a thousand years. The returnees rebuilt the altar and laid the temple foundation amid shouts of joy and the weeping of old men who remembered Solomon's temple (Ezra 3:10-13).

Opposition came quickly. 'The adversaries of Judah and Benjamin', people who had been settled in the north by Assyria and worshipped the LORD alongside other gods, offered to help and were refused (Ezra 4:1-3; compare 2 Kgs 17:24-33). They then frustrated the work for years. Ezra 4 also collects later letters of opposition from the reigns of Xerxes and Artaxerxes, arranged by theme rather than date, which can confuse readers. Prompted by Haggai and Zechariah, the people resumed building in 520 BC; when local officials questioned them, Darius found Cyrus' decree in the archives at Ecbatana and ordered the work funded (Ezra 6:1-12). The temple was completed in 516/515 BC and dedicated with Passover.

Decades later Ezra arrived with a royal letter authorising him to teach and enforce 'the law of thy God' (Ezra 7:25-26). Persian kings did support local law codes in their provinces, which helps explain his commission. Ezra had 'prepared his heart to seek the law of the LORD, and to do it, and to teach' (Ezra 7:10). His first major crisis was intermarriage: many returnees, including priests and leaders, had married women from surrounding peoples. Ezra's response, public mourning and a covenant to send away foreign wives and children (Ezra 9-10), is one of the most difficult passages in the Bible.
40399: Persia ruled through local elites and temples, supporting local religion and law as long as taxes were paid and order kept. The returnees depended on royal permission.
40401: The returned exiles called themselves the golah, the 'exile community', and saw themselves as the true remnant of Israel, distinct from those who had stayed in the land.
40403: Families proved their Israelite and priestly descent by written records. Those who could not were excluded from the priesthood until a priest with Urim and Thummim could decide.
40405: Aramaic was the language of Persian administration from Egypt to India. The book quotes letters and decrees in it, showing the community's dependence on imperial paperwork.
40407: Originally a royal secretary; Ezra becomes the model of the scribe as Torah scholar and teacher, a role that grows into the rabbis.
40409: Ezra calls Israel 'the holy seed' that has 'mingled' with the peoples, using the language of Lev 19:19 and Deut 7:3-4. Scholars debate whether the concern was ethnic, religious, or both.
40410:
In the Hebrew Bible, Ezra and Nehemiah are a single book in the Writings, placed just before Chronicles. Jewish tradition holds Ezra in enormous honour. The Talmud (Sanhedrin 21b) says that Ezra was worthy to have the Torah given through him, had Moses not come first. Tradition credits him with restoring the Torah to the people after the exile, introducing the square Aramaic script still used for Hebrew today, and leading the 'Men of the Great Assembly' who, according to the Mishnah (Avot 1:1), received the tradition from the prophets and passed it to the sages. The Talmud (Bava Kamma 82a) lists ten enactments attributed to Ezra, including the public reading of the Torah on Mondays, Thursdays and Sabbath afternoons, still practised in synagogues.

The first audience would have heard Ezra as a story of God's faithfulness after the worst disaster in their history. The God who had sent them into exile now 'stirred up the spirit' of a pagan emperor to send them home (Ezra 1:1), and 'the hand of the LORD his God' was upon Ezra (Ezra 7:6; Ezra 7:9; Ezra 7:28). The rebuilding of the temple and the restoration of Torah meant that the covenant relationship continued. The Passover kept at the temple's dedication included not only returnees but 'all such as had separated themselves unto them from the filthiness of the heathen of the land, to seek the LORD God of Israel' (Ezra 6:21), suggesting that the community was open to those who joined it in worship.

The intermarriage crisis was understood within the memory of what had led to exile. Solomon's foreign wives had turned his heart to other gods (1 Kgs 11:1-8), and Deuteronomy had warned that marriages with Canaanite peoples would lead Israel to serve their gods (Deut 7:3-4). For a tiny community surrounded by others, losing its distinct worship and language (compare Neh 13:23-24) seemed to threaten its very existence. Ezra's prayer of confession (Ezra 9:6-15) is a model of corporate repentance in which the leader identifies with the people's sin: 'our iniquities are increased over our head'.

40460: Ezra shows a return from exile that was real but incomplete: the people are back but still 'servants' under foreign kings (Ezra 9:9; compare Neh 9:36). Many scholars, including N. T. 40482:
By the mid-5th century BC the Jerusalem temple had stood for seventy years, but the city around it was thinly populated and unprotected. Walls in the ancient world were not only defence; they signalled that a city had status and honour. A city without walls was exposed to raids and shame: 'the remnant... are in great affliction and reproach' (Neh 1:3). Ezra 4:7-23 records an earlier attempt to rebuild that was halted by Artaxerxes himself after local officials accused the Jews of planning rebellion.

Nehemiah held one of the most trusted positions in the Persian court. A cupbearer tasted the king's wine to guard against poison and often became an adviser. When the king noticed his sadness, Nehemiah prayed silently and asked to be sent to rebuild the city (Neh 2:1-8). The king granted him letters, timber and an escort, and later appointed him governor. That a king who had once stopped the work now commissioned it is presented as 'the good hand of my God upon me' (Neh 2:8).

Opposition came from neighbouring officials: Sanballat the Horonite (governor of Samaria), Tobiah the Ammonite (possibly governor in Transjordan, with family ties to Jerusalem's priests) and Geshem the Arab (a powerful ruler named on a silver bowl found in Egypt). They used mockery, threats of attack, false rumours of rebellion, attempts to lure Nehemiah to a trap and a hired false prophet (Neh 4:1-3; Neh 6:1-14). The people built with tools in one hand and weapons in the other (Neh 4:17-18). The walls were finished in 52 days (Neh 6:15).

Nehemiah also faced an inner crisis. Wealthy Jews were charging interest and taking the children of poorer Jews as debt slaves during a famine and tax burden (Neh 5:1-5). Nehemiah was furious and forced the nobles to cancel debts and return property, while he himself refused the governor's food allowance (Neh 5:14-18). Then came spiritual renewal: Ezra read the Torah publicly from morning to midday, Levites explained it, the people wept and were told to celebrate, kept the feast of Booths, confessed their history in a long prayer, and signed a covenant (Neh 8-10). The book ends with Nehemiah's second term, in which he finds the old problems back: Tobiah lodging in the temple, Levites unpaid, Sabbath trading and mixed marriages in which children could no longer speak Hebrew (Neh 13).
40483: A royal official who served and tasted the king's wine; a position of great trust and personal access. Nehemiah risks his position by appearing sad before the king.
40485: Broken walls meant shame and vulnerability. Rebuilding them restored the city's honour among its neighbours, who then 'were much cast down in their own eyes'.
40487: Poor families mortgaged land and sold children into service to pay taxes and buy grain. The Torah forbade charging interest to fellow Israelites and limited slavery.
40489: Ezra reads from a wooden platform; Levites help the people understand, probably including translation into Aramaic and explanation. This became the pattern for synagogue reading.
40491: The people make a 'sure covenant' in writing, sealed by leaders, Levites and priests, committing to specific practices: no mixed marriages, Sabbath, sabbath year, temple tax, firstfruits and tithes.
40493: Nehemiah's short prayers ask God to remember his deeds, similar to inscriptions of ancient officials. They show an intimate, ongoing relationship with God amid action.
